subject: biology

items.q: Which feature is shared by all viruses?
items.correct: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
items.misconception: A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
items.why: At GCSE and MYP level viruses, bacteria, fungi and protists are taught together as 'microorganisms' or 'pathogens', and viruses are drawn as rounded bodies with an outer layer, so students file them as a kind of tiny cell. Everyday language about viruses 'feeding', 'living' and 'dying' reinforces this. A virus has no cytoplasm and no metabolism. It consists of DNA or RNA in a protein capsid, sometimes enveloped in host cell membrane, and it carries few or no enzymes. Everything a virus needs to be replicated, from ATP to ribosomes, is supplied by the host cell, which is why viruses are extreme obligate parasites and why whether they are 'alive' is a matter of definition.
items.specStatementText: What every virus has in common
items.random_wrong: A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer

items.q: A newly discovered particle 30 nm across contains one molecule of single-stranded RNA inside a protein shell. It has no ribosomes and it multiplies only inside living cells. How does the particle multiply?
items.correct: Its RNA and proteins are made by the host cell's machinery and then assembled into new particles.
items.misconception: It grows to about twice its size inside the cell and then divides into two identical particles.
items.why: Bacteria are taught alongside viruses, and binary fission is the only mode of microbial reproduction most students have met. Words such as 'reproduce' and 'multiply' in GCSE descriptions of viruses invite the assumption that the mechanism is division. Viruses have a small, fixed size. Inside the host cell the viral genome is copied and viral proteins are made by host ribosomes, and complete new particles are assembled at full size from these components. Because there is no growth and no division, the number of particles can jump from one to about a hundred in a single cycle.
items.specStatementText: What every virus has in common
items.random_wrong: It absorbs nutrients from the cell into its cytoplasm and metabolizes them to build copies of itself.

items.q: Which is a correct comparison of bacteriophage lambda and HIV?
items.correct: Lambda has double-stranded DNA and no envelope, whereas HIV has RNA and an envelope.
items.misconception: Both have an icosahedral head joined to a tail through which the genetic material is injected.
items.why: The bacteriophage is the iconic 'virus' image in textbooks and online, and it is the first virus most students study in detail, so its distinctive shape becomes the mental model for every virus. Teaching one exemplar in depth hides the range of forms. Bacteriophage lambda, coronaviruses and HIV show how different viruses can be. Lambda is a non-enveloped double-stranded DNA phage with a head and tail; coronaviruses are enveloped single-stranded RNA viruses with spike proteins; HIV is an enveloped retrovirus with two single-stranded RNA molecules and a cone-shaped capsid. Only a handful of features are common to all viruses.
items.specStatementText: Viruses differ widely in shape, genome and envelope
items.random_wrong: Both carry reverse transcriptase so that their genetic material can be copied into DNA.

items.q: A newly isolated virus is inactivated by detergents that dissolve lipid bilayers, whereas bacteriophage lambda is unaffected by the same detergents. What does this indicate about the structure of the new virus?
items.correct: It is enveloped in host cell membrane, a lipid bilayer lying outside its protein capsid.
items.misconception: It has a lipid envelope that it synthesized itself, using enzymes encoded in its own genome.
items.why: Everything else in a virus particle is coded for by the viral genome, and the name 'viral envelope' suggests something the virus owns. Students also do not connect the fact that viruses have no metabolism with the fact that they therefore cannot synthesize lipids. A virus has no enzymes for making lipids, so the envelope has to be taken from the host: as the assembled virus leaves the cell it is wrapped in a section of host membrane. This is why the IB describes such viruses as 'enveloped in host cell membrane'. The spike glycoproteins in the envelope are viral products, but the lipid bilayer is the host's.
items.specStatementText: Viruses differ widely in shape, genome and envelope
items.random_wrong: Its capsid is itself a phospholipid membrane, so the detergent dissolves the coat around its nucleic acid.

items.q: Which statement about the genetic material of viruses is correct?
items.correct: It is DNA or RNA, and either type may be single-stranded or double-stranded.
items.misconception: It is DNA in every virus, with RNA also present, as in a living cell.
items.why: In the central dogma as taught for cells, DNA is always the genetic material and RNA is a temporary messenger, and students have never met a system in which RNA is the inherited molecule. The general term 'nucleic acid' in the IB definition of a virus is read as 'both'. A virus contains one kind of nucleic acid as its genetic material. Bacteriophage lambda has double-stranded DNA; coronaviruses have single-stranded RNA that acts directly as messenger RNA; HIV has single-stranded RNA that is copied into DNA only after entering the host cell. Whichever molecule it is, it is the inherited genetic material of the virus.
items.specStatementText: Viruses differ widely in shape, genome and envelope
items.random_wrong: It is RNA in every virus, and is copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase.

items.q: In the lytic cycle of bacteriophage lambda, what happens after the phage has attached to a receptor on the surface of an E. coli cell?
items.correct: The phage DNA passes through the tail into the cell, and the capsid remains outside it.
items.misconception: The whole phage is taken into the cell and the capsid is broken down in the cytoplasm.
items.why: Animal viruses such as HIV, which are studied in the same topic, do enter the cell whole by fusion or endocytosis and are uncoated inside, so students apply the same picture to phages. Diagrams of the lytic cycle that show phages inside a bursting cell reinforce it. Bacteria have a cell wall that a phage cannot cross, so lambda acts like a syringe: the tail binds to a specific receptor protein and the DNA is injected into the cell while the empty capsid stays attached to the outside. Only the phage DNA is needed inside, because the host's machinery does everything else.
items.specStatementText: The lytic cycle: the host cell does the work, then bursts
items.random_wrong: The phage membrane fuses with the bacterial membrane, releasing the DNA inside.

items.q: A single lambda phage infects an E. coli cell in a large culture. Each lytic cycle takes 40 minutes and ends with lysis releasing 100 phages, every one of which immediately infects a fresh cell. How many phages are released by the lysis events that occur 120 minutes after the first infection?
items.why: Students picture the original infected cell as the only source of phages, releasing a batch per cycle, rather than each released phage starting its own infection. Rate calculations they have met before were linear, so they reach for addition. Every phage released at lysis can infect a fresh cell, so after n cycles the number of phages is (burst size) to the power n. With a burst size of 100, three cycles give 100 × 100 × 100 = 1 × 10⁶ phages, not 300.
items.specStatementText: The lytic cycle: the host cell does the work, then bursts

items.q: Bacteriophage lambda does not multiply in a sterile nutrient broth containing amino acids, nucleotides and ATP, but does multiply when living E. coli cells are added to the broth. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The phage lacks ribosomes and most enzymes, so it needs a cell's protein synthesis machinery.
items.misconception: The phage's own enzymes and ribosomes work only once they are activated inside a cell's cytoplasm.
items.why: Phrases such as 'the virus makes copies of itself' and 'the virus takes over the cell' picture the virus as the active agent doing the work, and a few viral enzymes (such as HIV's reverse transcriptase) are taught prominently, giving the impression that viruses are well equipped with enzymes. Viruses rely on a host cell for energy supply, nutrition, protein synthesis and other life functions. A phage genome inside a bacterium is transcribed by the host's RNA polymerase and translated on the host's ribosomes; the ATP comes from the host's cell respiration. This total dependence is why viruses cannot be cultured in a nutrient medium without living cells.
items.specStatementText: The lytic cycle: the host cell does the work, then bursts
items.random_wrong: The phage cannot absorb dissolved nutrients from the broth, but it can feed on the contents of a cell.

items.q: What happens to the DNA of bacteriophage lambda in the lysogenic cycle?
items.correct: It is integrated into the host chromosome and is copied along with it.
items.misconception: It stays as a separate circle in the cytoplasm, like a plasmid, replicating on its own.
items.why: Plasmids are the only extra pieces of DNA students have met in bacteria, and the lambda DNA does form a circle immediately after entering the cell, so a 'circle of foreign DNA in a bacterium' is naturally filed as a plasmid. In the lysogenic cycle a phage-encoded integrase inserts the circular lambda DNA into the host chromosome at a specific site. As a prophage it is part of the chromosome and is replicated by the host's DNA replication machinery along with it. It does not replicate independently and it is not a plasmid.
items.specStatementText: The lysogenic cycle: the phage genome hides in the host chromosome
items.random_wrong: It is transcribed slowly, making a few phages that leave the cell without lysis.

items.q: A culture of E. coli cells carrying the lambda prophage is growing normally. It is exposed to ultraviolet light, and about an hour later most of the cells lyse and release phages. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Damage to the host DNA induced the prophage to be excised from the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle.
items.misconception: The prophage had been releasing phages all along, and the ultraviolet light merely burst the cells.
items.why: Students learn that some animal viruses leave cells by budding without immediate lysis, and confuse this non-lytic release with lysogeny. The word 'cycle' also suggests that something is continually being produced. Lysogeny is a dormant state. The prophage sits in the chromosome, is copied when the cell divides, and produces no virions. Production of phages and lysis of the cell happen together, and only after induction switches the prophage into the lytic cycle.
items.specStatementText: The lysogenic cycle: the phage genome hides in the host chromosome
items.random_wrong: A prophage cannot cause lysis, so the culture must have been contaminated by a separate lytic phage.

items.q: All viruses are very small, have a protein capsid and depend completely on a host cell. How do biologists interpret these shared features?
items.correct: As convergent evolution: extreme obligate parasitism imposes the same demands on unrelated viruses.
items.misconception: As homologous features that all viruses have inherited from a single ancestral virus.
items.why: Students are taught to use shared characteristics to build cladograms and infer common ancestry, and the rule 'shared features imply relatedness' is applied without checking whether the features are homologous or convergent. Similar selective pressures produce similar features in unrelated organisms. Every virus is selected to be a minimal particle that can get its genome into a host cell and survive outside one, so a small size and a protective protein capsid are expected in any lineage that adopts this way of life. The IB states that these common features could be regarded as convergent evolution.
items.specStatementText: Viruses probably arose several times from cellular life
items.random_wrong: As ancestral features retained from the first living things, from which cells later evolved.

items.q: Viruses use the same genetic code as cellular organisms, yet their genomes may be single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA, whereas all cells have double-stranded DNA genomes. Which conclusion is consistent with both observations?
items.correct: Viruses are derived from cellular organisms, and probably arose on several separate occasions.
items.misconception: Viruses all descend from one ancestral virus, just as all cells descend from a single common ancestor.
items.why: Students learn that the tree of life has a single root and that every group of organisms is expected to be monophyletic, so they assume 'viruses' must also be a natural group with one origin. Viruses are not a single lineage. Different virus groups have genomes of different types and share very little, which is why the IB describes the evidence as pointing to several origins. The few features they have in common are better explained by convergent evolution under the same parasitic lifestyle than by common descent.
items.specStatementText: Viruses probably arose several times from cellular life
items.random_wrong: Viruses evolved before cells existed, and cells later inherited the genetic code from them.

items.q: Why do influenza viruses and HIV evolve so rapidly?
items.correct: Their genome-copying enzymes lack proofreading, and vast numbers of virions are produced quickly.
items.misconception: Their RNA genomes are chemically unstable, so bases change spontaneously between one infection and the next.
items.why: Students learn that messenger RNA is short-lived and that RNA is less stable than DNA, and they connect this instability with mutation rather than with the copying process. The real cause, proofreading during replication, is a detail of DNA polymerase that is easily forgotten. Mutations are copying errors. An RNA genome is not more likely to change while it sits inside a virion; it is more likely to be miscopied when it is replicated, because the viral polymerases do not check and correct the new strand. Combined with a short generation time and huge numbers of virions, this gives a very rapid rate of evolution.
items.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
items.random_wrong: They alter their genes deliberately whenever they are attacked by antibodies or by antiviral drugs.

items.q: Why must the influenza vaccine be reformulated with different strains every year, when the measles vaccine has stayed effective for decades?
items.correct: Point mutations change influenza's surface antigens each year, so earlier antibodies no longer bind to them.
items.misconception: Memory cells against influenza die within a year, so a new vaccine is needed to replace them.
items.why: Students generalise from 'booster' doses of other vaccines, which are given to top up immunity, and from the everyday idea that a flu jab 'wears off'. They assume the virus is the same each year and that only the immune response changes. Memory cells against a given antigen persist for years; the reason they do not protect is that the virus's haemagglutinin and neuraminidase have mutated, so the antibodies no longer bind. If the virus did not change, a single vaccine would give lasting protection, as the measles vaccine does. Reformulation, not just repetition, is needed because the antigens themselves have changed.
items.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
items.random_wrong: Reassortment of the genome segments produces a completely new influenza subtype every year.

items.q: HIV infection is treated with a combination of three antiretroviral drugs that act on different viral enzymes, rather than with a single drug. Why is a combination used?
items.correct: Resistance to one drug arises readily in the rapidly mutating population, but one virion is unlikely to resist all three.
items.misconception: One drug would eliminate the virus if it were taken for long enough; three are used only to shorten the course of treatment.
items.why: Students' experience of antimicrobial treatment is a course of one antibiotic that clears the infection, and they have not appreciated how quickly a population with HIV's mutation rate and size can produce a resistant variant. Treatment of a rapidly evolving virus has to prevent the selection of resistant variants, not just kill the sensitive ones. With one drug, resistant virions already present in the population survive and multiply, so the drug soon fails. Combination therapy targets several viral enzymes at once, and resistance to all of them would require several independent mutations in one virion.
items.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
items.random_wrong: HIV carries its own enzymes for every step of its replication, so all of them have to be blocked at the same time.

items.q: In 2009 a new strain of influenza A appeared with genome segments derived from swine, avian and human influenza viruses, and it caused a pandemic. Which process produced this strain?
items.correct: Reassortment of RNA genome segments in a cell infected by two different strains.
items.misconception: Gradual accumulation of point mutations in the haemagglutinin gene of one strain.
items.why: The two terms are similar-sounding technical words met together, and reassortment is the more striking mechanism, so students apply it to every change. The eight-segment genome is memorable, whereas point mutation seems too ordinary to explain annual changes. Annual changes are the result of antigenic drift: point mutations in the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes accumulate because the RNA polymerase lacks proofreading. Antigenic shift requires two different strains to infect the same cell and exchange segments, which produces a new subtype only occasionally, as in the 2009 H1N1 pandemic.
items.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
items.random_wrong: Reverse transcription of the viral RNA followed by insertion of host genes.

items.q: What is the capsid of a virus made of?
items.correct: Protein. The capsid is a coat of protein subunits around the nucleic acid. Some viruses additionally have a lipid envelope outside the capsid, derived from host cell membrane, but the capsid itself is protein in every virus.
items.misconception: The outer coat of a virus is a membrane made of phospholipid, so the capsid is a kind of cell membrane.
items.why: The only outer boundary students have studied in detail is the phospholipid bilayer of a cell membrane, and diagrams of viruses draw the capsid as a simple outline that looks like a membrane. Enveloped viruses such as HIV, which do have a lipid layer, are then generalised to all viruses. A capsid made of protein is one of the few features shared by all viruses. A lipid envelope is an extra layer present only in enveloped viruses, and even then it is taken from the host cell's membrane rather than being part of the capsid. Bacteriophage lambda has no lipid at all: its capsid is its outermost layer.
items.specStatementText: What every virus has in common

items.q: Do all viruses use reverse transcriptase to copy their genetic material into DNA?
items.correct: No. Only retroviruses such as HIV carry reverse transcriptase and make a DNA copy of their genome. Most RNA viruses, including coronaviruses, replicate their RNA directly using an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, and DNA viruses such as bacteriophage lambda have their DNA transcribed and replicated by host enzymes; neither has a reverse transcription step.
items.misconception: Every virus works like HIV: whatever its genetic material, it must be copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase before its genes can be used, so reverse transcriptase is a standard viral enzyme.
items.why: HIV is the RNA virus taught in most detail, and its reverse transcription step is memorable because it reverses the usual direction of the central dogma, so students generalise it to viruses in general, whatever their genetic material. Reverse transcription is a special feature of retroviruses. In a coronavirus the single-stranded RNA genome can be translated directly by host ribosomes and is copied RNA-to-RNA by a viral polymerase; in bacteriophage lambda the double-stranded DNA is transcribed and replicated by host enzymes. Genetic material may be RNA or DNA, single- or double-stranded, and the way it is copied differs between virus groups.
items.specStatementText: Viruses differ widely in shape, genome and envelope

items.q: Is a phage permanently either lytic or lysogenic?
items.correct: No. Bacteriophage lambda is a temperate phage: the same phage can follow either cycle, and a prophage can later be induced, for example by DNA damage from ultraviolet light, to leave the chromosome and enter the lytic cycle.
items.misconception: Lytic phages and lysogenic phages are two different kinds of virus, and once a phage genome has become a prophage it can never produce new phages.
items.why: The two cycles are usually drawn as two separate diagrams, and the names sound like two categories of virus. The dormant prophage, which visibly 'does nothing', is easily taken to be permanently inactivated. Lytic and lysogenic are two pathways open to the same virus. Lambda chooses between them after infection, and a lysogen can be switched to the lytic pathway by induction, so a bacterial population carrying a prophage can suddenly start releasing phages and lysing.
items.specStatementText: The lysogenic cycle: the phage genome hides in the host chromosome

items.q: Were viruses the ancestors of cells?
items.correct: No. Viruses are extreme obligate parasites that cannot be replicated without a host cell, and they use the same genetic code as cellular organisms; the evidence indicates that they are derived from other organisms rather than being their precursors.
items.misconception: Because viruses are so much simpler than cells, they must be the primitive first forms of life from which cells later evolved.
items.why: Students equate 'simple' with 'ancient', and the origin-of-life narrative of increasing complexity makes the smallest replicating thing seem the obvious starting point. The simplicity of viruses is not recognised as a consequence of parasitism. A virus has no metabolism and depends entirely on a host cell, so viruses in their present form could not have existed before cells. Their shared genetic code shows they are derived from cellular organisms, and their simplicity is the result of extreme obligate parasitism, in which anything the host can supply is dispensed with.
items.specStatementText: Viruses probably arose several times from cellular life

items.q: Do viruses change deliberately in response to drugs, vaccines or immune attack?
items.correct: No. Mutations arise at random during replication, regardless of any threat. Drugs, antibodies and immune cells then act as selection pressures: variants that happen to survive them leave more descendants, so the population changes.
items.misconception: A virus responds to a drug or vaccine by mutating in order to escape it, adapting on purpose to survive.
items.why: News reports and everyday speech say that a virus 'adapts', 'outsmarts' or 'evades' treatment, language that describes the outcome as if it were an intention. Lamarckian reasoning, in which organisms change because they need to, is a persistent intuition at every level. Rapidly evolving viruses generate huge numbers of random mutations because their replication is error-prone and their populations are enormous. A drug does not cause the resistance mutation; it removes the non-resistant virions and leaves the resistant ones, which then multiply. The virus has no goal and no mechanism for directing its mutations.
items.specStatementText: Why some viruses evolve so fast, and what that means for treatment
